extracted.intended_audience: aspiring New Yorker Caption Contest entrants and humor writers
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for writing and selecting captions to enter The New Yorker's weekly caption contest, focusing on brevity, correctly identifying speakers, narrative captions, originality, and premise-consistent surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word Economy
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep captions brief; shorter is better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical advice quoted: the 1912 San Francisco Call said 'the title must not exceed sixteen words' and emphasized 'the shorter the better.' Prioritize brevity — eliminate filler and unnecessary words to maximize punch and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctly identify the speaker (Who's Talking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine which character in the cartoon is delivering the line and make that clear in the caption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misidentifying the speaker breaks the joke or makes the caption nonsensical. The book chapter 'Who's Talking' focuses on this as a primary technical requirement for successful captions; ensure the voice and perspective match the drawn character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell a story — don't merely describe
rubrics_metrics.description: Write captions that advance or imply a narrative rather than just stating what is visible in the cartoon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rubric stresses 'Tell a Story' — captions should add context, cause, consequence, or a surprising twist rather than restating the scene. Story captions engage readers and are more likely to stand out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept the premise of the cartoon
rubrics_metrics.description: Work within the cartoon's premise, however outlandish, instead of rejecting or contradicting it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rubric item: 'Accept the premise of the cartoon, no matter how outlandish.' Counterproductive entries try to correct or argue with the cartoon's setup; good captions assume the cartoon's world and play inside it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caption must make sense within the premise
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the caption is coherent and logically consistent with the cartoon's characters, setting, and premise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rubric item: 'Caption must make sense within the parameters of the premise.' Even surreal cartoons have internal rules; the caption should not introduce contradictions that confuse rather than amuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose words carefully — eliminate unnecessary words
rubrics_metrics.description: Select precise wording and trim extraneous language to sharpen the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core topic 'Choose Your Words Carefully' and practical rubric item emphasize editing for precision. Replace vague or padded phrases with specific, punchy choices; brevity and diction both serve the surprise/punchline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find a unique angle — avoid the obvious read
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for a distinctive take that separates your caption from many similar submissions; avoid predictable or tired responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core advice: avoid being 'Too Predictable' or 'Too Unpredictable.' The winning caption example ('I will give you no quarter') succeeded because of precision and distinctiveness among 200+ similar entries. Seek novelty in perspective or phrasing rather than rehashing the obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for surprise (violate expectations appropriately)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use surprise — an unexpected twist or realization — as the essential humorous mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bob Mankoff's tip: 'Surprise is the essential ingredient in humor.' Surprise works by violating expectations and then resolving the tension so the reader realizes there's nothing to fear. Structure captions to set up an expectation and then deliver a lightweight, nonthreatening surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid obscenity, aggression, and cruelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid jokes that rely on obscenity, aggression, or cruelty as levers for humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mankoff notes New Yorker cartoons intentionally remove these levers. Practical rubric item: 'Aim for surprise without obscenity, aggression, or cruelty.' Steer clear of mean-spirited or offensive punchlines; the contest favors wit over nastiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and precision matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinctive phrasing and precise wording can make an entry win even among many similar submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical insight with example: when a cartoon drew 200+ similar captions, the winning entry 'I will give you no quarter' succeeded because it was both precise and distinct from minor variants. Originality can be subtle — choose phrasing that stands apart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get feedback — test multiple entries
rubrics_metrics.description: Share several candidate captions with friends/family as judges to see which land best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice: 'Get Feedback.' Wood recommends testing multiple entries with informal judges to filter weaker captions and refine wording. Use outside readers to catch misreadings and to compare relative funniness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage expectations and persist
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect frequent rejection and persist — submit many entries over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wood submitted over 800 gags and lost often, yet achieved multiple wins and finalists. Treat the contest as probabilistic: volume, learning from losses, and persistence improve long-term outcomes rather than seeking immediate success.
